transcript:
User: Hello? Yeah... I got your card. You help with phones, right?
Agent: Yeah, that’s me — we help make sure you don’t lose business from missed calls.  

Got it, you mentioned a card… was that something Jay handed you in person, or did you find it somewhere else?
User: Uh, yeah, Jay gave it to me. Said you could help with calls going to voicemail.
Agent: Got it, so Jay handed it to you and you're looking for help with calls going to voicemail.  

When your calls go to voicemail right now, what's the biggest issue it creates for you — lost jobs, annoyed customers, something else?
User: Uh, I guess it's lost jobs mostly. Some customers get annoyed too, I think. Not sure how many.
Agent: Yeah, that makes sense — lost jobs and irritated customers add up, even if you can’t put a number on it.  

When a call comes in and you can’t grab it — are you usually out on a job, with another customer, or is it more after-hours?
User: Uh, mostly out on jobs or talking to other customers. Sometimes after-hours too, I think.
Agent: Gotcha, so it’s ringing while you’re busy working, and some slip through after-hours too.  

Those calls that hit voicemail now — do people usually leave a message, or do you think most just hang up and call the next guy?
User: Uh, some leave messages, but I think a lot just hang up and call someone else.
Agent: Yeah, that’s exactly where the lost jobs creep in — if they hang up, they’re usually gone.  

Roughly how many calls a week would you say are going to voicemail instead of getting picked up live?
User: Uh, I don't know, a bunch, maybe ten? fifteen?
Agent: Got it, so maybe 10–15 a week are hitting voicemail instead of you.  

What kind of work do you actually do — are you HVAC, plumbing, something else?
User: Uh, landscaping. We do lawns, gardens, and some tree work, mostly.
Agent: Nice, thanks — so you’re doing lawns, gardens, some tree work.  

With those 10–15 calls a week going to voicemail, are there certain ones that really sting when you miss them — like bigger cleanups, recurring maintenance, or emergency tree jobs?
User: Uh, yeah, the bigger cleanups and recurring maintenance ones, I think. Those are the ones that hurt more.
Agent: Yeah, that tracks — missing those bigger cleanups and repeat contracts really adds up over a season.  

Hearing all that, are you mainly looking for a way to make sure every one of those calls gets answered and booked, even when you’re out on a job?
User: Uh, yeah, that sounds right. Just want to make sure we don't miss any calls when we're busy.
Agent: Totally get it — you just want those calls caught and turned into jobs while you’re out making money.  

Has anyone ever actually walked you through what missing those 10–15 calls a week is costing you in real dollars?
User: Uh, no, never really thought about it in dollars. Just know it's lost business.
Agent: Yeah, totally get that — it just feels like “missed business” in the background.  

Mind if we do a super quick back-of-the-napkin math on it together, just to see what you’re actually leaving on the table?
User: Uh, I guess we can try. I'm not too good with numbers, but go ahead.
Agent: No worries at all — I’ll keep it simple.  

So ballpark, out of those 10–15 calls a week that hit voicemail, what percentage do you think would actually book a job if someone answered live — maybe half, like 50%, or more like 30%?
User: Uh, I have no idea — half? more?
Agent: Gotcha, let’s keep it simple and go with half for now.  

And on average, what’s a typical job worth for you — like a standard cleanup or maintenance visit, are we talking more like $300, $500, $800?
User: Uh, depends, maybe four hundred? or five?
Agent: Gotcha, let’s use four hundred to keep it simple.  

So with the numbers you gave me, you’re leaking around eighty-six hundred a month in work from missed calls — would it help if we showed you exactly how to plug that leak so those calls get answered and booked, even when you’re on a job?
User: Uh, yeah, that sounds important. I'd like to know more about how it works.
Agent: Makes sense — if you’re leaking that much, it’s worth really seeing how to stop it.  

So, instead of going deep over the phone right now, we do a quick 20‑minute walkthrough where Jay shows you exactly how it works and what your numbers look like with it turned on — what’s better for you, later today or sometime tomorrow?
User: Uh, tomorrow might be better. Need some time to think about it.
Agent: Makes sense, you’ve got a lot going on and this is about real money for you.  

Real quick though — if I could guarantee you 5 to 10 extra jobs a month by stopping those missed calls, would that be worth 2 minutes to get a walkthrough on the books for this week?
User: Uh, yeah, I think so. Can we maybe do that walkthrough tomorrow or later this week?
Agent: Yeah, we can definitely line it up for tomorrow or later this week.  

To get that set up, what’s your first name?
User: Uh, it's Pedro. Tomorrow or later this week sounds good. What time were you thinking?
Agent: Nice to meet you, Pedro.  

And your last name?
User: Uh, nice to meet you too. It's Gonzalez.
Agent: Thanks, Pedro Gonzalez, got it.  

And what’s the name of your landscaping company?
Agent: Got it.  

What’s the name of your landscaping company?
User: Uh, it's just Pedro's Landscaping. Nothing fancy.
Agent: Got it, Pedro's Landscaping — perfect.  

And is the number you’re calling from right now the best number to reach you, or do you use a different one for the business?
User: Uh, yeah, this number works. It's the one I use for the business too.
Agent: Perfect, we’ll use this one then.  

Quick check — are you on Eastern time, Central, Mountain, or Pacific?
User: Uh, we're on Eastern time here.
Agent: Perfect, Eastern time, got it.  

So I can get you in as soon as Thursday at 12:30 or 5:15 in the afternoon Eastern — which of those feels better for you?
User: Uh, let's go for Thursday at 12:30. That works for me.
Agent: Awesome, Thursday at 12:30 Eastern sounds good.  

Quick thing — what’s the best number to reach you on?
User: Uh, this number I'm on works fine. It's the one I use for business.
Agent: Gotcha, we’ll use this one.  

Oh sorry, I didn’t get your number quite right — could you read it out for me real quick, just the digits?
User: Uh, sure, it's 555-1234, I think.
Agent: Got it, thanks Pedro.  

And just to double-check I heard you right — is your full number +5551234, or is there a different area code in front of 555-1234?
User: Uh, yeah, it starts with 123. So it's 123-555-1234.
Agent: Mhm, thanks — that helps.  

Just to be totally sure the number’s right: could you say it for me one more time, nice and slow, from the very beginning, including the area code?
User: Uh, okay. It's 123, then 555, and 1234. You got that?
Agent: Perfect, thanks Pedro — that’s exactly what I needed.  

And just to confirm everything, you’re set for this Thursday at 12:30 Eastern with Jay, and he’ll call you right on that 123‑555‑1234 number — does that all sound good?
User: Uh, yeah, that sounds good. Thursday at 12:30 Eastern, and Jay will call me. Thanks.
Agent: Thanks, Pedro! You’ll get a text with the confirmation details so you can add it to your calendar or reschedule if you need to. Really glad you called in today — Jay’s looking forward to talking with you on Thursday. Have a great rest of your day!
